facts.fact_text: Following the 2003 Armenian presidential election, the applicant participated in a series of rallies of protest organised in Yerevan by the opposition parties.
On 7 April 2003 at 17h00 a demonstration was held in the centre of Yerevan on the occasion of Mother's Day.
The demonstration of 7 April 2003 appears to have been of a political nature, and criticism of the Government and of the conduct of the 2003 Armenian presidential election was voiced at it.
The applicant alleged, and the Government did not dispute, that the demonstration of 7 April 2003 was organised by women.
The applicant alleged, and the Government did not dispute, that the demonstration of 7 April 2003 was attended by about 30,000 people, the majority of whom were female.
The applicant did not as such participate in the demonstration of 7 April 2003, since most men, including himself, were observing it from a distance, standing on both sides of Mashtots Avenue.
The task of the men observing the demonstration of 7 April 2003 from a distance, including the applicant, was to encourage the women and to prevent possible provocations.
At the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the Deputy Head ordered the applicant to stop participating in the demonstrations.

According to the applicant, on his way home on 7 April 2003, about 100-150 metres away from the site of the demonstration, he was approached by two persons in civilian clothes who showed police identity papers.
According to the applicant, the two persons in civilian clothes who approached him on 7 April 2003 took him to the Central District Police Station of Yerevan.
At the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the arresting police officers drew up a record of the applicant's arrest (արձանագրությաւն բերման ենթարկելու մասին).

The record of the applicant's arrest stated that the applicant had been 'arrested at around 17h30 on the Mashtots Avenue for obstructing traffic and behaving in an anti-social way at a demonstration'.

The police officers drew up a record of an administrative offence (վարչական իրավախախտման արձանագրություն) stating that the applicant had 'participated in a demonstration, during which he violated public order'.
The applicant's actions were qualified under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences (Վարչական իրավախախտումների վերաբերյալ ՀՀ օրենսգիրք) as minor hooliganism.

Judge M. of the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan, after a brief hearing, sentenced the applicant under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences to three days of administrative detention.

The police officers drew up a record of an administrative offence (վարչական իրավախախտման արձանագրություն) stating that the applicant had 'participated in a demonstration, during which he violated public order'.
The applicant's actions were qualified under Article 172 of the Code of Administrative Offences (Վարչական իրավախախտումների վերաբերյալ ՀՀ օրենսգիրք) as minor hooliganism.
The applicant alleged that he had initially refused to sign the record of an administrative offence and requested a lawyer.

The applicant alleged that his initial refusal to sign the record of an administrative offence and his request for a lawyer was the reason why he was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan for the following five and a half hours.

The applicant alleged that during the period he was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan, the police officers were persistently trying to convince him to sign the record of an administrative offence and to refuse a lawyer.
The applicant alleged that the police officers told him it was unnecessary to have a lawyer and spend money for such a minor case.

The applicant alleged that the police officers told him the case had been already pre-decided by their superiors, so a lawyer would only harm rather than help, and that he may end up spending quite some time at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan because of that.

The applicant alleged that the police officers told him that if he signed the record of an administrative offence and refused a lawyer, he would be immediately taken to a court, where at worst a small fine would be imposed and he would be released.
The applicant alleged that he finally succumbed and agreed to sign the record of an administrative offence and to refuse a lawyer.

The Government contested the applicant's allegation that he was kept at the Central District Police Station of Yerevan for five and a half hours under pressure to sign the record of an administrative offence and refuse a lawyer.
According to the Government, the record of an administrative offence was signed by the applicant voluntarily and without any objections.

The judge's entire finding in the applicant's case amounted to the following sentence: 'On 7 April 2003 at around 17h00 ... on the Mashtots Avenue [the applicant], together with a group of people, obstructed street traffic, violated public order by making a loud noise, and incited other participants of the demonstration to do the same...'
According to the record of the court hearing, no questions were put to the applicant.

The applicant alleged, and the Government did not explicitly dispute, that the record of the court hearing was a fake and was drafted at some point after the hearing in order to create an appearance of lawfulness.
The applicant alleged that the hearing lasted only about five minutes and was conducted in judge M.'s office.
The applicant alleged that, contrary to what the record of the court hearing stated, only judge M., the applicant and the accompanying police officer were present at the hearing.
The applicant alleged that judge M. listed the materials prepared by the police and asked the applicant 'what do you want?', to which the applicant replied 'Justice and lawfulness'.

The applicant alleged that judge M. continued reading through the materials and said 'since you have three children and have not been guilt-stained in the past, I will impose a mild sentence of three days of detention'.
The applicant alleged that in reply he tried to present the circumstances of the case, petitioned judge M. to summon some witnesses and requested a lawyer.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that in most cases, hearings lasted from a few seconds to a few minutes and the written judgments were pre-prepared.

According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant said that he blocked traffic because it was a demonstration and everybody else was doing the same.
According to the record of the court hearing, the applicant said he made noise since everybody else was making noise, but he did not push anybody.
According to the record of the court hearing, no questions were put to the applicant.

According to the record of the court hearing, having familiarised himself with the materials prepared by the police, the applicant accepted that he had signed the record of an administrative offence but objected to being subjected to administrative liability since the incriminated acts had been committed also by others.

The Constitutional Court of Armenia stated that subjecting persons to administrative detention for having participated in unauthorised demonstrations and marches constituted an interference with the right to freedom of peaceful assembly guaranteed by Article 11 of the Convention.
The Constitutional Court of Armenia stated that such application of the administrative detention procedure was in contradiction with European 'rule of law' standards.

The Report by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Committee on the Honouring of Obligations and Commitments by Member States of the Council of Europe, Doc. 10027, dated 12 January 2004, states that the day after the first round of the presidential election held on 9 February 2003, several demonstrations and protest meetings took place in Yerevan and several towns at the prompting of opposition political parties.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that between the two rounds of the 2003 Armenian presidential elections, and as from 22 February 2003, more than 200 people were arrested by the police at the behest of the authorities, among them some members of the political parties in opposition or of their campaign staff, and agents of these parties.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that the arrested persons were taken into custody without notification of their families, then brought before the courts and sentenced to a fortnight's administrative internment in over 80 cases, or to fines in 65 other cases.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that the persons arrested between the two rounds of the 2003 Armenian presidential elections were tried in camera and with few exceptions did not receive the assistance of a lawyer.
The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that many of the arrested persons were unable to participate in the second round of the 2003 Armenian presidential election.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that further arrests were made after the second round of the 2003 Armenian presidential election, with the Ministry of Justice acknowledging that 132 people were arrested between 17 and 25 March 2003, 69 of them being sentenced to an 'administrative' custodial penalty and 63 to a fine.
The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that according to the OSCE, 77 is the number sentenced to a term of imprisonment over the period of 17 to 25 March 2003.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 describes the summary procedure prescribed by the Administrative Code of Armenia as an authentic remnant of the Communist style of justice inherited from the Soviet era, which denies the person charged the right to inform his/her family or to request the immediate assistance of a lawyer, and enables a judge, under an arrangement for immediate trial in camera, to have him/her held for a fortnight maximum.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that during an August 2003 visit, the Armenian authorities justified their decision to arrest and convict demonstrators by invoking the need to shield law and order from their misdeeds, claiming that the demonstrators were thugs, 'antisocial elements', alcoholics or drug addicts.

The Report Doc. 10027 of 12 January 2004 states that the freedom to demonstrate and the freedom to come and go must be reconciled with respect for law and order, and that preservation of law and order must not serve to condone wrongful deprivation or restriction of freedom to form assemblies and to demonstrate.

Resolution 1361 (2004) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe on honouring of obligations and commitments by Armenia states that the Assembly is shocked by the scandalous use that continues to be made of the arbitrary procedures concerning administrative detention provided for in the Administrative Code of Armenia, which is totally incompatible with Resolution 1304 (2002).

Resolution 1361 (2004) of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe firmly condemns the arrest and conviction of over 270 people — members of the opposition parties, sympathisers and office-holders — between the two rounds of the 2003 Armenian presidential election and at the end of the second round.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 titled 'An Imitation of Law: the Use of Administrative Detention in the 2003 Armenian Presidential Election' states that in the period between the 19 February 2003 round and the 5 March 2003 runoff of the presidential election, the main opposition candidate's campaign staged several rallies in the centre of Yerevan, each of which attracted tens of thousands of supporters.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that after the 5 March 2003 runoff the main opposition candidate's campaign continued to stage rallies in the centre of Yerevan at intervals of several days or a week, to protest alleged election fraud.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that although rallies and protest demonstrations in support of the main opposition candidate were largely peaceful, the governing authorities portrayed them as a threat to public order and political stability, and used this as grounds for arrests.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that several men and women were arrested after the 7 April 2003 demonstration in central Yerevan and given administrative fines or terms of detention.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that on bringing opposition activists to the police station, officers kept them in incommunicado detention, depriving them of counsel, which allowed police wide scope to pressure the activists to admit guilt.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that in almost all cases, administrative court hearings against opposition activists were closed and cursory, with courts considering only police evidence and not giving the defendant the opportunity to summon defence counsel or defence witnesses.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that several factors indicate that the judges acted under the influence of political authorities, including that in many cases judges issued the harshest administrative sentence possible — fifteen days detention — to opposition activists.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that some judges at the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan were frank with defendants about their one-sentence-fits-all policy, with one judge telling a defendant 'Those who took part in the rally — we are giving them all fifteen days' and another stating that 'his instructions were to put us all away for fifteen days — no less.'

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that judges' questioning of several defendants was blatantly political, such as 'Why do you play at opposition?' and 'Why do you bad-mouth the government?', and that judges warned some not to participate in opposition rallies again.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that during the week of 22-28 February 2003, when the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan tried nearly one hundred supporters of the main opposition candidate, 'Red Berets' — police commandos — sealed off the building to the public, and the chairman of the court acknowledged that their deployment was an initiative of the police leadership on which the court was not consulted.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that some defendants demanded lawyers but court officials and police told them that lawyers were either 'not necessary' or 'not allowed' in administrative cases, and that lawyer N.B. was barred from entering the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan on 22 February 2003 to defend his client despite having a contract with the defendant.
The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that in most cases, hearings lasted from a few seconds to a few minutes and the written judgments were pre-prepared.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that one judge started a defendant's hearing by reading out his sentence — fifteen days detention for having participated in an unauthorised march — and when the defendant objected that he had not participated in the march, the judge said 'It is proven' and called a policeman to take him away.

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that two opposition party activists from the Shengavit district of Yerevan were each given three days' detention without learning what they were charged with, and that a judge quelled another defendant's objection to the absence of stated information or grounds for his fifteen-day sentence with the comment 'Just say thank you that we didn't press a criminal charge.'

The Human Rights Watch Briefing Paper of 23 May 2003 states that on 22 February 2003 the Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan handed out some administrative detention sentences without conducting hearings in the presence of defendants, with at least one police van with several detained activists inside seen to drive up to the court where a court official emerged and reportedly handed prepared judgments to the escorting police officers, after which the van drove away without the defendants having set foot in court.
